topics: 🔑 Resolving Rami bar Ḥama's Dilemmas — who adds the fifth, who performs temurah
🐄 New Mishna: No Substituting Limbs for Fetuses, or Fetuses for Whole Animals
🤰 Bar Padda vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan — are fetuses sanctified when consecrated?
⚖️ Rabbi Zeira vs. Rabbi Yirmeya — testing bar Padda against mishna after mishna
💰 Kedushat HaGuf vs. Kedushat Damim — how strong is 'value-sanctity' alone?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Whose Offering Is It, and What Can Be Consecrated
overview.subtitle: Temurah 10a–10b
overview.hebrewSource: מַקְדִּישׁ מוֹסִיף חוֹמֶשׁ, וּמִתְכַּפֵּר עוֹשֶׂה תְּמוּרָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves two dilemmas of Rami bar Ḥama that trace back to the opening of the tractate: when one person consecrates an offering for another's atonement, the consecrator alone adds the redemption fifth, but the one achieving atonement is the one who performs substitution. A new mishna then turns to a different boundary of temurah: one cannot substitute non-sacred limbs for a consecrated fetus, or vice versa, or either for a whole animal (with Rabbi Yosei partly dissenting). This launches a long-running dispute between bar Padda and Rabbi Yoḥanan over whether a fetus can be directly imbued with sanctity at all — argued out through a marathon exchange between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Yirmeya, who test bar Padda's position against mishna after mishna, ultimately distinguishing sanctity that inheres in an animal's body from sanctity that inheres merely in its value.

slides.title: 🔑 Two Dilemmas About 'Whose' Offering It Is
slides.subtitle: One person consecrates; another achieves atonement with it

steps.content: 1️⃣ Dilemma one: if it later becomes blemished and is redeemed, who adds the one-fifth — the consecrator or the one who atones?
2️⃣ Answer: 'And if HE WHO CONSECRATED will redeem his house' (Lev. 27:15) — only the consecrator adds a fifth, never the one who merely atones
3️⃣ Dilemma two: who can perform temurah for it — the consecrator or the one who atones?
4️⃣ Answer (R' Abbahu, citing R' Yoḥanan): the one who ACHIEVES ATONEMENT performs temurah — not the consecrator

callout.label: Full circle:
callout.text: This is the very question left open on daf 2 — whether ownership for temurah follows the consecrator or the one atoning. It is now resolved: it follows the one atoning.

slides.title: 🐄 New Mishna: Limbs, Fetuses, and Whole Animals Don't Mix
slides.subtitle: Four combinations barred, with Rabbi Yosei's partial exception
rows: Does take effect — the whole substitute becomes holy

callout.label: Rabbi Yosei's proof:
callout.text: Just as saying 'this animal's leg is a burnt offering' consecrates the whole animal, saying 'this leg is a substitute' should make the whole animal a substitute.

slides.title: 🤰 Can a Fetus Itself Be Sanctified?
slides.subtitle: Bar Padda and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree at the root

lines.speaker: Bar Padda
lines.text: Sanctity does not take hold on a fetus directly — it isn't yet a complete 'animal.'

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yoḥanan
lines.text: Sanctity does take hold on a fetus. Proof: if one consecrates a pregnant sin offering and it gives birth, he may choose to bring either the mother OR the offspring for atonement — the other then grazes until blemished.

lines.speaker: Question
lines.text: Why state this twice — once for consecrating the mother while pregnant, once for consecrating the fetus alone? Either case should teach the same halakha!

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Each case needs its own teaching: consecrating the mother might extend to the fetus only because the mother herself is fit; consecrating the fetus alone might not work since it isn't 'outside' yet. Both are necessary.

callout.label: Stakes:
callout.text: This dispute over fetal sanctity directly explains the new mishna's rule that fetuses cannot serve as, or be substituted by, ordinary animals.

slides.title: ⚖️ Rabbi Zeira Defends Bar Padda, Mishna After Mishna
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yirmeya presses with proof after proof; Rabbi Zeira distinguishes each

nodes.content: ❓ R' Yirmeya: a mishna on avoiding firstborn status says 'what's in this womb, if male, is a burnt offering' — and it works when born! Doesn't that prove fetuses take sanctity?
💬 R' Zeira: that is only value-sanctity (קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים) — sold, proceeds fund an offering — not inherent bodily sanctity
❓ R' Yirmeya presses: is value-sanctity even strong enough to cancel firstborn status, or to forbid working the mother?
✅ R' Zeira: yes — animals blemished before consecration are exempt from firstborn law and gifts only until redeemed, proving value-sanctity alone suspends both
❓ R' Yirmeya: what about offspring already born of a consecrated mother (וַלְדֵי קָדָשִׁים) — clearly sanctified!
✅ R' Zeira: different — sanctified through the mother's consecration, not through direct consecration of a fetus

callout.label: Ongoing debate:
callout.text: The exchange runs through several more mishnayot, each requiring its own fine distinction to preserve bar Padda's position.

slides.title: 💰 Kedushat HaGuf vs. Kedushat Damim
slides.subtitle: Two levels of sanctity, with very different strength

boxes.title: קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף (Inherent/Bodily)
items: The animal itself must be sacrificed
Applies to a properly consecrated unblemished offering
Bar Padda: cannot apply to a fetus directly

boxes.title: קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים (Value/Monetary)
items: Only the animal's sale-value is sacred; proceeds buy an offering
Can apply even to a fetus, per bar Padda
Still strong enough to cancel firstborn status and forbid labor before redemption

callout.label: Key move:
callout.text: By conceding that value-sanctity can apply to a fetus, bar Padda answers every challenge — each proof-text turns out to describe value-sanctity, not the inherent sanctity Rabbi Yoḥanan claims.

summary.principle: The one who achieves atonement — not the consecrator — performs temurah, while a fetus can acquire only value-sanctity (not inherent bodily sanctity), explaining why the mishna bars substitution between limbs, fetuses, and whole consecrated animals.

flowSteps.content: 🔑 Consecrator adds the fifth; the one atoning performs temurah — Rami bar Ḥama's dilemmas resolved
🐄 New mishna: limbs, fetuses, and whole animals cannot substitute for one another (R' Yosei partly dissents)

columns.content: 🤰 Bar Padda: no inherent sanctity on a fetus; R' Yoḥanan: there is
💰 Bar Padda's escape hatch: value-sanctity CAN apply to a fetus

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: every proof for fetal sanctity is reinterpreted as mere value-sanctity, preserving bar Padda's rule

quiz.q: According to the resolution of Rami bar Ḥama's dilemmas, when one person consecrates an animal for another's atonement, who performs temurah for it?
o: The consecrator
The one who achieves atonement with it
Neither can perform temurah
Both must agree together
quiz.e: Rabbi Abbahu, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, rules that the one who achieves atonement (מִתְכַּפֵּר) — not the consecrator — is the one who can effect substitution, resolving the dilemma raised back on daf 2.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei's dissenting view in the new mishna, in which case does substitution actually take effect?
o: Substituting a limb for a fetus
Substituting a non-sacred limb for a whole consecrated animal — the entire substitute becomes holy
Substituting a fetus for a limb
None of the cases work according to Rabbi Yosei
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei holds that just as declaring an animal's leg a burnt offering consecrates the whole animal, declaring a non-sacred limb a substitute for a whole consecrated animal renders the entire substitute holy.

quiz.q: What is the core dispute between bar Padda and Rabbi Yoḥanan?
o: Whether animals can be consecrated at all
Whether a fetus can be directly imbued with (inherent) sanctity when consecrated
Whether priests can perform temurah
Whether gentiles can consecrate animals
quiz.e: Bar Padda holds sanctity cannot take hold directly on a fetus; Rabbi Yoḥanan holds it can, citing the case of a consecrated pregnant sin offering where either the mother or the offspring can be brought for atonement.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Zeira defend bar Padda against the mishna about avoiding firstborn status (saying 'what's in the womb is a burnt offering')?
o: He says the mishna is incorrect
He explains it refers only to value-sanctity (kedushat damim), not inherent bodily sanctity
He says fetuses are never affected by that mishna
He agrees it refutes bar Padda
quiz.e: Rabbi Zeira consistently reinterprets each challenge as describing value-sanctity (sanctity of the fetus's monetary worth) rather than the inherent bodily sanctity that bar Padda denies can apply to a fetus.

quiz.q: According to the mishna about animals blemished before consecration, what shows that value-sanctity (kedushat damim) alone is strong enough to have real legal force?
o: Nothing — value-sanctity has no legal force
Such animals are exempt from firstborn law and priestly gifts only until they are redeemed, after which those obligations apply
They are immediately eaten without restriction
They can never be redeemed
quiz.e: The mishna implies that before redemption, animals with only value-sanctity are exempt from firstborn status and gifts, proving that even this lesser sanctity is strong enough to override those obligations while it lasts.
